I couldn't find the TIME article itself on content.time.com, so these results are secondary sources that confirm the award and its context.

- **The award:** TIME named the PET/CT scanner its medical invention of the year for 2000. The PET/CT scanner, developed by Townsend and Ronald Nutt, PhD, was named by TIME Magazine as the medical invention of the year 2000.
- **Timing:** One Siemens account says the prototype was unveiled at the RSNA meeting in Chicago in November 2000, and TIME's recognition followed that December (In November 2000, the new scanner was unveiled to the world at the Radiological Society of North America's (RSNA) annual meeting in Chicago, Illinois, USA.).
- **The inventors:** A CERN Courier piece names the two co-inventors and identifies Nutt's role. The other is engineer Ronald Nutt, senior vice president and director of research and development at CTI PET Systems – the leading supplier of PET technology – in Knoxville, Tennessee. Townsend is the physicist, and the CERN piece notes his earlier time at CERN.
- **Origin:** Townsend's idea reportedly began with a call to Nutt. "So, I called Nutt at CTI and asked him, 'How about adding CT to PET?'"

The sources also date the idea and prototype differently. One says the idea arose in 1991 in Geneva (DOTmed), while Siemens says the prototype was built by 1995 at Pittsburgh. The TIME article's own wording and category name ("Medical Invention of the Year") would need to be checked against the original piece.

Alternatively, EXPLORER can scan with a radiation dose up to 40 times less than a current PET scan, opening new avenues of research and making it feasible to conduct many repeated studies in an individual, or dramatically reduce the dose in pediatric studies, where controlling cumulative radiation dose is particularly important. “The tradeoff between image quality, acquisition time and injected radiation dose will vary for different applications, but in all cases, we can scan better, faster or with less radiation dose, or some combination of these,” Cherry said. For example, it could quantitatively measure blood flow or how the body takes up glucose everywhere in the body. The search points to a correction to the premise: Gemini TF was first unveiled in March 2006, not at the June 2006 SNM meeting. SNM was where Philips showcased it that June.

- **March 2006 launch:** Philips released the system at the European Congress of Radiology in Vienna on March 3, 2006 (Philips Medical Systems released the world's first commercial time-of-flight PET/CT system March 3 at the European Congress of Radiology in Vienna.). The company's own release called it the world's first commercially available time-of-flight PET/CT system. That is Philips' claim, not an independent verification.
- **June 2006 SNM:** At the SNM annual meeting in San Diego, the system was shown alongside JETStream Workspace 3.0. Philips described it as the first PET/CT system to market that features TruFlight technology. AuntMinnie reported that full commercial release of the system was expected by the end of June 2006.
- **TruFlight:** AuntMinnie said Gemini TF uses what Philips calls TruFlight technology, the company's term for time-of-flight imaging.
- **Later status:** By SNM 2007, Philips reported more than 30 installations worldwide of the system.

I did not find the original Philips press release text itself, only trade-press coverage that reproduces or summarizes it.

Yes, the search confirms the core claim. Several sources say Time named the PET/CT scanner its medical invention of the year for 2000, and attribute it to David Townsend and Ronald Nutt. One source, a Time citation dated December 4, 2000, credits the article to L. Jaroff and calls the honor "Medical Science Invention of the Year." The results don't show the full Time article text.

- **Recognition:** A Journal of Nuclear Medicine interview says the scanner was named by TIME Magazine as the medical invention of the year 2000. The Engineering and Technology History Wiki gives the same award and year.
- **Credit:** Several sources name Townsend and Nutt as the developers. A Siemens Healthineers history places the honor in December of the same year.
- **Citation:** The Berkeley PET/CT page cites Jaroff, L. Time Magazine (2000, December 4).
- **Patent dispute:** A separate IP Advocate page reports that the patent was contested. It says the patent was not accepted until 2002, well after the two companies were competing in the marketplace.

I found nothing about "Kher" in these results, and nothing confirming the word "merged" as the article's wording. The closest match is a line describing the PET/CT concept as the merging not simply of images but of the imaging technology. That line comes from a conference-style slide deck, not the Time article. To verify the exact Time wording or any Kher connection, you'd need the original December 2000 Time article.

Links: [{"title":"A Winning Combination - TIME","url":"https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,998685,00.html"},{"title":"A new world order: training clinicians for a new era in imaging","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3097817/"},{"title":"The quest for the ideal anato-molecular imaging fusion tool","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3097821/"},{"title":"Method and apparatus for determining depth of interactions in a detector for three-dimensional complete body screening","url":"https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/7217928"},{"title":"NEMA NU 2-2018 performance evaluation of a new generation digital 32-cm axial field-of-view Omni Legend PET-CT","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.06255"},{"title":"TIME Magazine -- U.S. Edition -- December 4, 2000 Vol. 156 No. 23","url":"https://content.time.com/time/magazine/0,9263,7601001204,00.html"},{"title":"Portable positron emission tomography scanner having a rotatable detector ring which can be rotated 90 degrees for imaging a patient in a vertical or horizontal configuration","url":"https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/10653374"},{"title":"Positron computed tomography scanner","url":"https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/5291021"},{"title":"State of the art in total body PET","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7248164/"}]

The search turned up the TIME article you're looking for, though not any mention of an "Invention of the Year" award.

- **The article:** Leon Jaroff's piece ran in TIME's December 4, 2000 issue, in the "Inventors & Inventions" special report. Electrical engineer Ronald Nutt and physicist David Townsend, working at the University of Geneva in Switzerland developed the combined machine. The article describes how it merged the two scanners. Two Americans working in the Alps come up with a plan to merge two widely used scanning devices--the PET and the CT--into one.
- **Timeline:** The pair later moved to the University of Pittsburgh. They received a three-year, $1.5 million grant from the National Cancer Institute in 1995 that enabled them to complete a prototype machine. TIME reported that the new scanners will be installed at Manhattan's Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, Indiana University, the University of Iowa and other medical facilities by early 2001.
- **Commercialization:** One review credits Townsend's group with the pioneering work and dates the combined systems to 1998. Commercial release followed: GE went on to release the first commercial PET/CT in 2001, followed soon after by Siemens.

The search did not confirm the award wording, so verify that against the TIME issue itself. The results also give different dates for the early development work (1995 grant versus 1998 pioneering), so treat those as approximate.

Subscribe Sign In --> Subscribe A Winning Combination Two Americans working in the Alps come up with a plan to merge two widely used scanning devices--the PET and the CT--into one By Leon Jaroff Monday, Dec. 04, 2000 Share Tweet Read Later Send to Kindle Email Print Share Facebook Twitter Tumblr LinkedIn StumbleUpon Reddit Digg Mixx Del.i.cious Google+ Reprints Follow @TIME The idea came out of left field. Electrical engineer Ronald Nutt and physicist David Townsend, working at the University of Geneva in Switzerland, had just taken the cover off their newly developed metabolic-imaging machine and were admiring its innards when an oncology surgeon happened by. "You have a lot of space between those detectors," he offered. "You ought to try to put something in there that would be useful." At the time, eight years ago, PET (positron emission tomography) machines, which can reveal subtle metabolic processes such as tumor growth, and CT (computerized tomography) scanners, which show precise anatomical details, were already in widespread medical use. But doctors, especially cancer surgeons, were often frustrated in their attempts to match the two different scans to determine, for example, the precise location of a tumor in relation to an organ or to the spinal column. There seemed to be no better way than simply "eyeballing" the two separate images. That is, until Nutt and Townsend had their epiphany in the Alps. Last October the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the marketing of a combination PET/CT machine, the first medical-imaging device that simultaneously and clearly reveals both anatomical details and metabolic processes within the body. By early next year the new scanners will be installed at Manhattan's Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, Indiana University, the University of Iowa and other medical facilities. --- @3264: ead medical use. But doctors, especially cancer surgeons, were often frustrated in their attempts to match the two different scans to determine, for example, the precise location of a tumor in relation to an organ or to the spinal column. There seemed to be no better way than simply "eyeballing" the two separate images. That is, until Nutt and Townsend had their epiphany in the Alps. Last October the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the marketing of a combination PET/CT machine, the first medical-imaging device that simultaneously and clearly reveals both anatomical details and metabolic processes within the body. By early next year the new scanners will be installed at Manhattan's Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, Indiana University, the University of Iowa and other medical facilities. Others had attempted, with little success, to match the two different images by using computer algorithms as a way to unify data from CT and PET scans made at different times and in different settings. "The problem is that the body is kind of a flimsy structure," says Nutt, co-founder of CTI, the Knoxville, Tenn., imaging company that is gearing up to produce the new scanning combine. "If you lay it on the bed one time for a CT scan and another time for a PET scan, just a small difference in body position will result in all of the organs shifting about a bit, so it's very difficult to do that matching." After refining their combined PET and CT concept for three years, Nutt and Townsend, who had transferred from the University of Geneva to the University of Pittsburgh, received a three-year, $1.5 million grant from the National Cancer Institute in 1995 that enabled them to complete a prototype machine. Installed at the University of Pittsburgh medical center in 1998, it has been used successfully to scan some 200 patients. In many of these cases, says Dr. Carolyn Cidis Meltzer, who with Townsend is a co-director of the University of Pittsburgh pet facility, the use of the PET/CT machine has resulted in decisions to modify or change treatment. In one case a standard CT scan had detected a tumor on the left side of a patient's neck but none elsewhere. "When CTs are read and you look for a spread of tumor to the lymph nodes," Meltzer explains, "all you're able to look at is the size of the lymph node." If a CT shows that a lymph node is less than one centimeter in size, it is considered to be normal. But on the PET/CT, Meltzer says, "we saw a very small lymph node in the right side of the neck that we thought was involved with the tumor." A biopsy that otherwise would not have been performed confirmed her suspicion. Received 2019 Jan 23; Accepted 2019 Jan 24. © 2019 by the Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging. PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC6424228 PMID: 30733314 Abstract Within the EXPLORER Consortium, the construction of the world’s first total-body PET/CT scanner has recently been completed. The 194-cm axial field of view of the EXPLORER PET/CT scanner is sufficient to cover, for the first time, the entire human adult body in a single acquisition in more than 99% of the population and allows total-body pharmacokinetic studies with frame durations as short as 1 s. The large increase in sensitivity arising from total-body coverage as well as increased solid angle for detection at any point within the body allows whole-body 18 F-FDG PET studies to be acquired with unprecedented count density, improving the signal-to-noise ratio of the resulting images. Alternatively, the sensitivity gain can be used to acquire diagnostic PET images with very small amounts of activity in the field of view (25 MBq, 0.7 mCi or less), with very short acquisition times (∼1 min or less) or at later time points after the tracer’s administration. We report here on the first human imaging studies on the EXPLORER scanner using a range of different protocols that provide initial evidence in support of these claims. These case studies provide the foundation for future carefully controlled trials to quantitatively evaluate the improvements possible through total-body PET imaging. Keywords: instrumentation, PET, EXPLORER, FDG, PET/CT, total-body PET Current-generation clinical PET/CT and PET/MR scanners typically cover an axial extent of 15–30 cm. Large increases in signal collection efficiency can be realized through extending the axial extent of the scanner, with the highest collection efficiency being approached as the scanner becomes long enough to cover the entire human body. A further key motivating factor for increasing the axial extent so dramatically is that it becomes possible to perform total-body dynamic studies, where tracer kinetic modeling with an image-derived input function to estimate model microparameters can be performed across all the organs and tissues of the body with high temporal resolution. Thus, the idea of developing long-axial-field-of-view (FOV) scanners, and ultimately total-body scanners, has been studied over many years and has recently gained increasing traction ( 1 , 2 ). NOTEWORTHY First human studies on the EXPLORER total-body PET scanner have been performed. The search results support the main points, though they don't give an exact date for the first patient scan at UC Davis.

- **Arrival and first patient:** UC Davis Health reports that Gonzalez, a 49-year-old mother of seven, became the first clinical patient in the world to be scanned on EXPLORER at the new EXPLORER Molecular Imaging Center on Folsom Blvd. in Sacramento. The same page says the scanner has since been used on about 200 patients and 65 research subjects.
- **Arrival:** A spring 2019 UC Davis Health article says the scanner will be operational this summer. It describes the EXPLORER Imaging Center occupies leased space on Folsom Boulevard.
- **FDA clearance:** The spring 2019 article states the FDA approved the technology in December. Since that issue is from spring 2019, this likely means December 2018, but the source doesn't name the year. A later interview also says the scanner is FDA cleared and is being manufactured by United Imaging.
- **Naming:** A UC Davis explorer page describes the uEXPLORER scanner, the first clinically approved total-body PET system in the United States, was installed in 2019.
- **Earlier human images:** The first human scans were made public in November 2018, with the team working with United Imaging Healthcare. The Journal of Nuclear Medicine paper reporting them appeared in March 2019.

The results don't give the exact date of the first patient scan, so I couldn't confirm that from these sources.
